sourceRequirements: The client’s total and subscale scores are expressed as percentiles based on normative data for Non-Autistic adults of the same gender (e.g., male, female, or gender diverse) (English et al., 2024).
The percentiles contextualise the client’s scores relative to the typical scores of Non-Autistic adults.

For example, the 50th percentile represents the typical levels of autistic traits among Non-Autistic adults, while scores on the 90th percentile fall within the top 10% when compared to Non-Autistic adults.

The total scale score reliably distinguishes between Non-Autistic and Autistic people, with cut-off scores calculated through statistical analyses that maximise the chances of correctly classifying Autistic people as Autistic and minimise the chances of incorrectly classifying Non-Autistic people as Autistic (English et al., 2024).
The total scale cut-off scores are as follows.
All : 148 and above (88th percentile and above among Non-Autistic adults; 25th percentile and above among Autistic adults)
Males: 139 and above (77th percentile and above among Non-Autistic Males; 25th percentile and above among Autistic Males)
Females: 141 and above (86th percentile and above among Non-Autistic Females; 13th percentile and above among Autistic Females)
Gender Diverse: 156 and above (87th percentile and above among Non-Autistic Gender Diverse adults; 22nd percentile and above among Autistic Gender Diverse adults)

It is important to acknowledge that the differing gender-specific cut-off scores may reflect systemic factors, including biases in referral and assessment processes, as well as gender differences in the presentation of Autism and likelihood of diagnostic overshadowing.
The higher cut-off scores for gender diverse individuals and cisgender females, in particular, may stem from historical underdiagnosis within these groups.
The cut-off scores reflect current diagnostic criteria and practices and are subject to change as the understanding, characterisation, and assessment of Autism continue to evolve.

Percentiles are the primary metric for presenting scores because they are comparable across constructs, regardless of the number of items, and are readily communicated to clients and other professionals.
Each score is converted to a percentile against the distribution of scores on that construct in a reference sample drawn from Forbes et al.’s (2025) study.
Percentiles can be based on the whole reference sample, All (respondents aged 16 years and over), or on one of two subsets of it, Youth (16 to 24 years) and Adult (25 years and over).
Percentiles therefore describe the client’s standing relative to that population rather than the general community.
A score at the 50th percentile is typical of that population and does not indicate an average level of psychopathology relative to the general community.
A distress-enriched sample has the advantage that its percentiles discriminate among individuals across the full range of severity, including the high levels seen in clinical settings.
The percentile does not itself say whether a level of psychopathology is clinically significant; that judgement is carried by the severity band.
The percentile instead shows how far the client’s level of psychopathology is from what is typical of the reference sample.
This means a percentile compares the client with people who may have been experiencing mental health difficulties, rather than with the general population.
A percentile around 50 means a typical level of psychopathology for that group, not an average level for the community.

descriptions.spectrum:Detachment: Measures disengagement from social and emotional life, together with low mood: reduced interest and pleasure, hopelessness and diminished self-worth, withdrawal from relationships and social contact, and a muted or unexpressed emotional range. In this measure, the dimension also encompasses reduced interest in sexual and romantic relationships.
descriptions.spectrum:Eating Pathology: Assesses disturbances of eating and body image, including fear of weight gain, the influence of weight or shape on self-evaluation, restrictive eating, and distress associated with overeating.
descriptions.spectrum:Externalising: Measures behaviour and emotion directed outward against other people, rules, or norms — a broad spectrum spanning impulsive, reckless, or aggressive conduct, manipulation and self-interest, reduced concern for others, and outwardly directed anger.
descriptions.spectrum:Harmful Substance Use: Assesses the core features of problematic alcohol and other drug use, including craving, loss of control over use, tolerance and withdrawal, continued use despite harm, and use in dangerous situations.
descriptions.spectrum:Internalising: Represents the broad propensity to experience negative emotions turned inward. This wide-ranging spectrum spans low mood, worry and anxious arousal, fear-based avoidance, social withdrawal, and trauma-related distress with disturbed sleep.
descriptions.spectrum:Mania: Measures the dimension of elevated and expansive mood. In this measure, it is assessed through euphoric mood, heightened sociability and talkativeness, unrestrained emotional expression, and enjoyment of attention.
descriptions.spectrum:Neurodevelopmental and Cognitiv: Encompasses difficulties of neurodevelopment and cognition — a broad spectrum spanning social communication, attentional and sensory regulation, ritualised and inflexible behaviour, and problems with memory, attention, and everyday cognitive functioning.
descriptions.spectrum:Somatoform: Assesses the experience of physical symptoms and bodily concern — pain, palpitations and breathlessness, temperature sensations, unsteadiness and slowed thinking or movement — together with health anxiety and disturbances of sleep and eating.
descriptions.spectrum:Thought Disorder: Measures disruptions to the ordinary integration of perception, thought, and consciousness, spanning psychotic-like experiences and beliefs, dissociative experiences, and associated physical and behavioural changes.
descriptions.subspectrum:Cognitive Difficulties: Assesses problems with everyday cognitive functioning: attention and concentration, memory, word-finding, planning and decision-making, mental speed, and the capacity to manage everyday tasks, possessions, and living spaces.
descriptions.subspectrum:Neurodevelopmental: Captures traits and difficulties commonly associated with neurodevelopmental conditions: social communication difficulties, overactivity and pressured speech, sensory sensitivity, unusually intense interests, and ritualised or inflexible behaviour.
descriptions.subfactor:Antagonism: Measures self-interested and manipulative interpersonal behaviour, including deceit, entitlement, attention-seeking, and deliberately annoying others.
descriptions.subfactor:Antisocial Behaviour: Represents the dimension of aggressive and harmful conduct. In this measure, it is assessed through physical aggression towards people, animals, or property.
descriptions.subfactor:Callousness: Assesses reduced empathy and emotional responsiveness to others: indifference to others' feelings, lack of concern about causing hurt, and a sense of personal superiority or entitlement.
descriptions.subfactor:Disinhibition: Measures deficient restraint over behaviour: acting without regard for consequences, recklessness, carelessness, and feeling or acting out of control.
descriptions.subfactor:Externalised Negative Affect: Captures negative emotion directed outward at other people and circumstances: irritability, anger and verbal outbursts, resentment, mistrust of others, and blaming others for one's own difficulties.
descriptions.subfactor:Distress: Represents the core negative-affect dimension of internalising — a broad blend of low mood and diminished pleasure, worry and anxious arousal, emotional lability, guilt and negative self-evaluation, and suicidality.
descriptions.subfactor:Dysregulated Sleep and Trauma: Assesses post-traumatic distress together with disturbed sleep: distress and avoidance connected to a traumatic experience, and difficulty falling or staying asleep.
descriptions.subfactor:Fear: Measures the phobic aspects of anxiety: fear and avoidance cued by particular objects, situations, or concerns — public or enclosed spaces, social scrutiny, specific phobic stimuli, illness and dying, bodily appearance, and rejection or abandonment.
descriptions.subfactor:Social Withdrawal: Assesses behavioural disengagement from social life — avoidance of and discomfort in social situations, anxiety about public spaces or being away from home, and diminished interest in other people — alongside lowered mood and enjoyment.
descriptions.subfactor:Difficulties with Organisation: Assesses difficulty keeping one's possessions and living environment manageable: losing needed items, clutter that limits the use of living areas, difficulty discarding possessions, and needing help with everyday household tasks.
descriptions.subfactor:Forgetfulness: Measures changes in memory and familiar abilities: difficulty recalling recent events, declining ease with familiar skills, and trouble finding one's way in familiar places.
descriptions.subfactor:Neurocognitive Impairment: Assesses a broad range of cognitive difficulties spanning attention, concentration, multitasking, memory, word-finding, mental speed and effort, planning and decision-making, and independence in daily activities.
descriptions.subfactor:Altered Sensation and Attentio: Measures dysregulation of attention, activity, speech, and sensory experience: restlessness and overactivity, pressured or excessive speech, sensitivity to sensory input, and unusually intense interests.
descriptions.subfactor:Ritualised Behaviour: Assesses rigid and repetitive patterns of behaviour: insistence on sameness, perfectionism, and repetitive acts performed to manage intrusive thoughts or distress, or to prevent something bad from happening.
descriptions.subfactor:Social Communication Difficult: Measures difficulty understanding and using communication in social interaction: following what others mean, holding reciprocal conversations, responding when others make contact, reading and using non-verbal cues, and adapting behaviour to the social context.
descriptions.subfactor:Dysregulated Eating: Represents the dimension of disrupted eating patterns that present alongside other physical symptoms. In this measure, it is assessed through eating large amounts of food in the absence of hunger.
descriptions.subfactor:Dysregulated Sleep: Assesses disturbance of the sleep–wake cycle as a physical presentation: difficulty falling or staying asleep, and excessive daytime sleepiness despite adequate sleep.
descriptions.subfactor:Somatic Symptoms: Measures the experience of distressing bodily symptoms — pain and muscle tension, palpitations and breathlessness, temperature sensations, unsteadiness and slowed thinking or movement — together with anxiety about one's physical health.
descriptions.subfactor:Dissociative Experiences: Assesses disruptions to the ordinary integration of consciousness, perception, memory, and identity: detachment from oneself or one's surroundings, gaps in memory, experiences of separate self-states, and sudden losses of control over thought, emotion, or behaviour.
descriptions.subfactor:Positive Psychosis: Measures psychotic-like experiences and beliefs: perceptions that others do not share, beliefs held despite contrary evidence, experiences of thought interference, and thinking or behaviour that others find strange.
descriptions.subfactor:Uncontrollable Physical Sympto: Assesses involuntary movements and unusual bodily sensations: trembling, chills, numbness or tingling, unsteadiness, and a sense of being slowed. In this measure, the dimension also encompasses being seen by others as odd or unusual.

A reliable change is one large enough to be unlikely to reflect measurement noise: 6 points or more on the Total, and 2 points or more on each subscale (Murphy et al., 2016; Kamin et al., 2015; McCarthy et al., 2016).

In practice, a reliable change without a band shift (e.g., a Total score moving from 8 to 14, both within the typical and Mild ranges) suggests a meaningful change in symptoms worth discussing with the family but does not constitute a positive screen.

Scores are presented as percentile ranks based on age-specific normative data for four groups: 5-6 years, 7-8 years, 9-10 years, and 11-12 years.
Percentiles indicate the child’s position relative to same-aged peers in the normative sample.

A percentile of 50 indicates that the symptom level for the child is at average and expected levels for a child of that age group and a percentile of 90 indicates that the child has relatively high symptom levels compared to their peers (i.e., higher than 90 percent of their peers).

The clinical cutoffs use the symptom count approach where behaviours rated as “often” or “very often” are flagged as a significant symptom with clinical cutoffs based upon meeting both threshold numbers AND functional impairment (Items 48-55).
Note, there can sometimes be discrepancies where a child might not meet the clinical cutoff but their percentile could be high (at the 90th percentile or higher).

The other reason this might happen is that the client scores high on a small number of symptom questions but then very low on others and even though they might have functional impairment, the actual threshold using the symptom count approach used for the clinical cutoff falls just short.
On first administration of the VADPRS, there are two plots shown.
The first horizontal bar plot shows the ADHD subtype raw scores with the normative and clinical samples shaded in the background (with the samples shown as between the 25th and 75th percentiles).

The normative percentile sample is the same as those used to derive the percentiles (i.e., the Anderson et al., 2022 sample) whereas the clinical percentiles are derived from a NovoPsych sample of over 3,000 children who met the clinical cutoff criteria.
The second plot shows the normative percentiles for all subscales with a coloured background at the 90th percentile and above, indicating elevated scores.
A line is presented on this plot at the 50th percentile which indicates an average symptom level for each of the subscales.
Subsequent administrations of the VADPRS show two longitudinal plots showing (i) the ADHD subtype raw scores and (ii) the comorbid percentiles over time.

sourceRequirements: Raw scores (sum of Likert response options), symptom scores, clinical cutoff descriptors (whether meeting the diagnostic criteria or not), and percentiles (based upon the symptom counts) are provided for the following subscales of the VADTRS:

However, the percentiles are based upon symptom counts (the number of items rated as “often” or “very often” for each subscale) and are derived from the original normative sample of over 8,000 elementary school children from the Wolraich et al.
Percentiles are calculated separately for male and female students, with combined norms used when gender information is not available.
Percentiles indicate the child’s position relative to same-gender peers in the normative sample based on their symptom count.

A percentile of 50 indicates that the symptom count for the child is at average and expected levels for a child of that gender, and a percentile of 90 indicates that the child has relatively high symptom counts compared to their peers (i.e., higher than 90 percent of their peers).

The clinical cutoffs use the symptom count approach where behaviours rated as “often” or “very often” are flagged as significant symptoms, with clinical cutoffs based upon meeting both threshold numbers AND functional impairment (Items 36-43).

To address this potential bias, the VADTRS interpretive system includes gender-equivalence flagging that identifies cases where female students may warrant further clinical evaluation despite not meeting traditional diagnostic thresholds.

Specifically, when a female student’s symptom count falls below the diagnostic threshold but her percentile rank matches or exceeds that of males who do meet diagnostic criteria (90th percentile for inattentive symptoms, 95th percentile for hyperactive/impulsive symptoms), the interpretive text will include a clinical note highlighting this discrepancy.

This flagging system recognises that percentile ranks may represent clinical significance across genders, and ensures that clinicians are alerted to potentially significant symptoms that might otherwise be overlooked in female students, thereby supporting more equitable diagnostic practices.
On first administration of the VADTRS a plot shows the normative percentiles for all subscales with a coloured background at the 90th percentile and above, indicating potentially elevated scores.
A line is presented on this plot at the 50th percentile which indicates an average symptom level for each of the subscales.
Subsequent administrations of the VADTRS show longitudinal plots showing the ADHD subtype raw scores and comorbid percentiles over time.

Note the coloured shading in the background of both plots represents symptom severity, not necessarily whether a client meets diagnostic criteria or not (given this is dependent upon functional impairment too).

For example, the 50th percentile represents the typical/“Normal” level of depressive symptoms among people aged 16 years and over, while scores on the 90th percentile fall within the top 10% when compared to people aged 16 years and over and are indicative of “Mild to Moderate” depressive symptoms.
